analysis.one_liner: Eliminates tax deductions for moving US jobs and equipment overseas and repeals the foreign tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the House Ways and Means Committee after its sole sponsor, Rep. Jim Jontz, introduced it with no cosponsors in April 1992.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the tax code in two ways. First, companies closing a US operation and moving the equipment and workers overseas could no longer deduct the cost of the move, the overseas pay of relocated employees, or depreciation on the shipped-out equipment. Second, it would repeal the foreign tax credit, the rule that lets US companies subtract foreign income taxes from what they owe the IRS — meaning multinationals would pay US tax on top of foreign tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in communities facing plant closings, because companies could no longer write off the costs of relocating operations abroad, making offshoring somewhat more expensive. The Treasury would also gain revenue from multinationals that currently offset foreign taxes against US tax.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could no longer deduct expenses for moving property or employees outside the US when reducing US operations, raising the cost of relocating jobs abroad [S2][S3].
Deductions for overseas pay of relocated employees and for depreciation on property moved offshore would be denied as long as that property stays outside the US [S2][S3].
Repealing the foreign tax credit would end the practice by which US companies subtract taxes paid to foreign governments from their US tax bill [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinationals moving operations or equipment out of the US, which would absorb relocation costs undeducted, and all US companies with foreign operations and foreign tax bills, which could face double taxation — paying tax on the same income to a foreign government and to the US.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the foreign tax credit outright goes far beyond plant-closing policy: every US company earning income abroad would pay tax on the same money twice — once to the foreign country, once to the US — which most tax experts consider double taxation and which could push companies to relocate headquarters rather than operations [S3].
The deduction denial applies only to the costs of moving out; it does not bar offshoring itself, so companies could still move jobs and simply absorb the unrecovered costs [S2][S3].
Because the bill had no cosponsors and was never drafted into a larger tax bill, it received no hearing or analysis of its economic side effects before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — stop subsidizing the paperwork of moving US jobs abroad — was aimed at a real and widely felt problem in the early 1990s. But the bill as written was blunt: its full repeal of the foreign tax credit would have hit every US company with overseas income, not just plant closers, and could have produced double taxation and unintended responses. The one-sided design and total lack of cosponsors meant it never got the committee scrutiny needed to test whether the benefits outweighed those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Jontz introduced the bill on April 30, 1992 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinationals kept the ability to deduct offshoring costs and to credit foreign taxes against US tax; US workers gained nothing from a bill that died unnoticed.

for.name: Rep. Jim Jontz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 30, 1992; it was his lone bill action.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill expired in committee.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, oversaw the panel that took no action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote and no recorded opposition, so no party split is visible; the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died without action.

industries.note: The bill would deny deductions for the costs of moving operations and equipment offshore and repeal the foreign tax credit, making offshoring more expensive and raising US tax on foreign income. Industry preference for keeping these tax benefits ran against workers whose jobs were being relocated.
